note: Round 3 changes lookback 252 -> 126, leverage 1 -> 1.5, and replaces max drawdown in the score with annual volatility (annual return 20%, annual volatility 10%, failure rate 70%). The round-2 parameters were therefore re-derived rather than inherited; nothing carries over by default. (1) anchor_penalty 4.0 -> 16.0. Round 2 picked 4.0 under a drawdown-heavy score; round 3 weights annual return twice as heavily as volatility, so the return end of the frontier is worth more, and on sp500 and factors the score rises monotonically with the penalty. Measured in one clean opponent pool (research/round3/select_r3.py), p=16 scores 0.6073 mean / 0.5783 worst against the twelve reference submissions, versus 0.5969 for p=4 and 0.5887 for the best reference method. p=32, 64 and 1e6 give the same 0.6073 except that 1e6 reaches 0.6140 by winning one more rank position on sp500; 1e6 is the ceiling and eliminates the variance term entirely, so p=16 is shipped instead, keeping the objective a genuine anchored variance problem rather than a restatement of its own anchor. (2) half_life 63 -> 30, i.e. a quarter of the window rather than a quarter of 252. The parameter is weakly identified at recent_mix 0.25 because the decay scale only rescales the volatility block, never the correlation structure: across half_life 16/21/30/42 the sp500 annual return spans 0.11pp and the resulting rank is unchanged (reports/round3_decay.json). The round-2 convention was kept and its insensitivity is recorded rather than presented as a tuned optimum. recent_mix stays at 0.25 even though 0.15 and 0.40 both score one rank position higher on ftse100 (0.6073 vs 0.5999 mean): the gap is a single rank step inside the field-resampling noise band established in round 2, and 0.40 would put 40% of the covariance weight on a recency block estimated from a 126-day window at half_life 30, which is a robustness cost the failure counts cannot see. The underlying effect is recorded rather than hidden: raising recent_mix from 0.15 to 0.40 lifts annual return on all three datasets (sp500 15.835% -> 16.026%, ftse100 13.610% -> 13.934%, factors 11.498% -> 11.583%) with volatility essentially flat, which is the favourable direction under a 20%/10% weighting; it was still not taken because the score difference is one position and the estimate is noisier. (3) gross_leverage is frozen at 1.0, NOT the brief's 1.5. The brief's number is a cap, not a requirement, and the measurement says the budget costs more than it buys: because the book is always fully invested, net exposure is 1 and gross is 1 + 2*(aggregate short), so a cap of 1.5 grants an aggregate short budget of 0.25 -- and using it lowers both return and volatility by roughly the same amount (ftse100 at p=4: annual -0.542pp, volatility -0.498pp). At the score's 20%/10% weights a 1:1 trade is a losing trade, and the budget lowered the score at every one of the seven penalties tested on the cross-dataset mean. It is also a robustness liability: at a low penalty the optimizer uses the budget to its exact limit, so gross sits at 1.500 and floating-point roundoff could carry it over the cap. The parameter is exposed, so enabling it is a one-number change plus a rebuild.
short_selling_note: The permission to short is implemented as an aggregate budget, not a per-asset floor, because the rule it enforces (gross exposure) is aggregate: a per-asset cap of c would bound the total short only by n*c, which grows with the universe. The projection onto {sum(w)=1, sum(max(-w,0)) <= s} is exact and closed form, verified against an independent KKT bisection to 1.1e-15 and against cvxpy to 5.7e-09, and the duality-gap bound g_min + s*(g_min - g_max) is verified against an LP to 6.0e-12 and shown to be a genuine lower bound (tools/round3_short_projection_check.py). At gross_leverage 1.0 the budget is zero and the code path is the long-only one. The previous round's leverage=1 made shorting arithmetically impossible; round 3's 1.5 makes it possible, and this round is the first in which the measurement, not the arithmetic, is what declines it.
